Use one force convention throughout. In independent generalized coordinates
$z=(q,\eta)$, let $v=\dot z$ and write

$$
M(z)\dot v+h(z,v)=\bar B(z)u,\qquad
h=Cv+\nabla_z V+d,\qquad \bar B=\begin{bmatrix}B\\0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Here $h$ contains the terms written on the left of the mechanical balance;
their signed contribution to acceleration is $a_d=-M^{-1}h$.
Known external loads must either be included with their signs in $h$ or
declared separately. These are the standard forward/inverse dynamics
conventions [@lynch2017modern; @featherstone2008rigid].

**Inverse dynamics estimates the applied generalized load.** Its output is

$$
\tau_{\mathrm{ID}}=\mathrm{ID}(z,v,\dot v)=M\dot v+h=\bar B u.
$$

Consequently, $\mathrm{ID}(z,v,a_d)=0$ for an exactly matched zero-input
model, up to numerical error. It does not return a nonzero gravity, elastic,
or interaction-force contribution. A constrained model can simultaneously
have zero actuator torque and nonzero constraint reactions; the solver's
actuator and reaction outputs must be distinguished.

**A resultant-force partition is a different quantity.** If we retain
$\tau_{\text{total}}$ for the net generalized right-hand side of $M\dot v$,
the consistent definitions are

$$
\tau_{\text{total}}:=M\dot v,
\qquad \tau_{\text{drift}}:=-h=M a_d,
\qquad \tau_{\text{input}}:=\bar B u=\tau_{\mathrm{ID}}.
$$ {#eq-tau_split}

Thus

$$
\tau_{\text{input}}=\tau_{\text{total}}-\tau_{\text{drift}}
=M(\dot v-a_d).
$$ {#eq-tau_input_def}

These symbols denote generalized loads, whose units depend on the coordinate:
torque for an angle, force for a translation, and the corresponding conjugate
load for a normalized modal coordinate. They are not individual muscle forces.
The rigid rows require the **full** acceleration vector:
$[M_{qq}\ M_{q\eta}]a_d$ includes recoil; $M_{qq}(a_d)_q$ alone does not.

For example, an unforced pendulum at an inclined angle has nonzero gravitational
acceleration. Applying inverse dynamics to that free fall returns zero pivot
torque. Holding it stationary instead requires the gravity-balancing torque.
The same distinction persists in a coupled golfer–club model.

A forward ZTCF follows its own state after release. In a shared local chart,

$$
\frac{d}{dt}(x-x_0)=f(x)-f(x_0)+G(x)u,
$$

where $x_0$ is the zero-input trajectory, not the initial-state symbol in this
equation. Only at a common state does the drift difference vanish. A later
trajectory difference contains the accumulated effect of changed geometry,
velocity, deformation, and contact; it is not an instantaneous input-force
sample. Specify the output, comparison time or event, horizon, and admissible
input set before interpreting closeness to a ZTCF as control authority.
